items.title: Charles "Creole Charlie" Levy Interview, 1962-01-03
items.q: I got Milton Hinton... I got him Hinton on bass, myself on the little guitar, and Wyatt Houston on violin. We went out this roadhouse and stampeded the place.

ctx.x: There were quite a few of you fiddlers around in the early years. Now you went to banjo, what happened to the rest of them? They tried to make it to the middle of the fiddle.

Wyatt Houston was one of them that was a classical fiddler that turned to jazz and he really could play it. He played all the Joe Van Nudie stuff. Is that so? And all the Eddie Saw's stuff. I tell you what we did, we had a job. The booking agent asked me, he says, can you get a little string band together? There's no piano in the roadhouse. We're out at 111th Street. I said, yes, I'll get you. So I got Milton Hinton. You know he's big in New York now. I got Milton Hinton. He was in school, still in school. He'd…
I remember when I go like when you had the trill.

items.title: Charles "Creole Charlie" Levy Interview, 1962-01-03
items.q: So we jobbed on the north side with the little trio, my wife, Houston, myself, and Milt Hinton.

ctx.x: He knew so much. In the wintertime.

And he had tremendous. And then he was a student of it, too. And he had a fast ear and he picked up stuff that the trumpets would play and he'd slide his fingers on the strings, you know, and to the plane he'd slide it and he'd twist the strings, shove the strings in like you do on the banjo, see. Make a quarter tone, see. Yeah. And we did pretty good until, I don't know, I think the prohibition agents or something happened and they came in and we had to get another job. We went down and made an audition at NBC.…
Would you give up fiddle in this period that you've mentioned? Yes.
